title: Hope, not fear
hook: Christian hope is trust that God finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a brass-band song and a multitude no one could number. Your line was in that number. Who did you make feel counted? Day one thousand three hundred twenty.

The letter was written in chains. Paul tells the church at Philippi that his "bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace." He writes as a man who might live or die; a few lines later he weighs both, and says he's torn. You'd expect a letter like that to open with worry, or with a request for help. Instead, almost the first thing he writes is a sentence with no doubt in it at all, about somebody else's unfinished life. This block has walked through Revelation's beasts and trumpets and endings. Today's word is what some Christians say all of it is meant to give.
screen: `A SENTENCE WITH NO DOUBT IN IT.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence: "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." Perform, in the old English, means carry it through to the end. Notice where the confidence sits. Not in the Philippians, who are still a work in progress. Not in Paul, who's in prison. It rests on the one who began. Second, hope isn't the same as optimism. Paul in bonds isn't forecasting good news; he says plainly, "to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." And Paul tells the Romans, "hope that is seen is not hope." Hope looks past what can be seen yet, to who holds the ending. Third, hope and fear. Revelation can be read as a book of threats, and some people have met it that way. But this block has kept arriving at the same places: all things new, open gates, healing leaves, come, Lord Jesus. The first letter of John says, "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." Fear asks what will go wrong. Hope asks who is finishing the story. Fourth, unfinished people. Begun a good work. Paul isn't embarrassed that the Philippians are half-built. He expects it. Some Christians bring this verse to people in the middle of things: a recovery, a grief, a slow change that hasn't arrived. The work isn't done. On Paul's account, it will be.
screen: `HE WHICH HATH BEGUN WILL PERFORM IT.`
`HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: replace one fear with hope. Settle, and breathe. Let one worry about something unfinished come up: your health, a child, your work, yourself. Don't rehearse it; just let it be there. Then look for one thing in that same place that has already been begun: a first step taken, a small mercy, someone who showed up. Hold that beside the fear. You don't have to make the fear disappear. Just let the beginning sit next to it. If you pray, you can rest on Paul's words, he which hath begun a good work. If you don't, just keep both in view and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Hope. Not a guess that things will turn out fine, but trust, written from chains, that the one who began a good work will carry it through.
Your line: he will finish it. Today, when you catch yourself bracing for the worst about something unfinished, name one thing already begun in it. Day one thousand three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Christians name hope among faith, hope and love (1 Corinthians 13:13), and some memorize Philippians 1:6 or pray it for people going through a long, unfinished season.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in bonds, not sure whether you'll live or die. you're writing to a young church you love. how do you open?

with confidence that the one who began a good work in them will finish it.

original.note: Greek: hope, expectation. the word Paul uses for hope, as in "hope that is seen is not hope", Romans 8:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: hope means expecting things to turn out fine.
what it means: Christian hope trusts that God finishes what he begins, even when the writer is in chains.
what a scholar hears: elpis, hope; and in Philippians 1:6, epitelesei, he will bring it to completion, all the way to the end.

notes: Philippians is treated as written while Paul was in bonds (from 1:13); where and when is left out. Confirm.
'He's torn' paraphrases Philippians 1:23 ('I am in a strait betwixt two'). Confirm.
'Perform, in the old English, means carry it through to the end' glosses the KJV word; Greek ἐπιτελέσει. Confirm.
'Revelation can be read as a book of threats, and some people have met it that way': general, softened; confirm.
'Some Christians bring this verse to people in the middle of things': general claim about use; soften if needed.

Editor: 'the thing Christians say all of it is meant to give' softened to 'some Christians'; the practice's 'name one fear ... say it once' reworded so it doesn't repeat day 1317's 'name the fear once'.
